content: The field of inorganic carbon chemistry encompasses a vast array of compounds containing carbon atoms. It is estimated that there are nearly ten million known carbon-containing compounds, though the actual number may be even greater. Organic Compounds Every organic compound contains at least one carbon atom. The number of organic compounds is immense, with approximately ten million defined compounds currently known. However, the theoretical number of possible organic compounds is far larger. Interestingly, some compounds that are typically classified as organic are occasionally considered inorganic. Examples of such compounds include ammonium carbamate (NH2COONH4), phosgene (COCl2), thiophosgene (CSCl2), thiourea (CS(NH2)2), and urea (CO(NH2)2). Inorganic Compounds Inorganic carbon chemistry refers to the study of carbon compounds that do not fall under the category of organic chemistry. Compounds with Nonmetals The most well-known inorganic carbon compounds are the oxides of carbon, such as carbon dioxide (CO2) and carbon monoxide (CO). Other less common oxides include carbon suboxide (C3O2), dicarbon monoxide (C2O), and the rare carbon trioxide (CO3). Binary compounds of carbon with other nonmetals include carbon disulfide (CS2), beta-carbon nitride (β-C3N4), carbon tetrabromide (CBr4), carbon tetrachloride (CCl4), carbon tetrafluoride (CF4), carbonyl fluoride (COF2), carbonyl sulfide (COS), and carborane (H2C2B10H10). Compounds with Metals Carbonic acid (H2CO3) is the only known acid derived from carbon oxides. When carbonic acid loses a single proton, it forms bicarbonates, which can further lose another proton to form carbonates. Examples of bicarbonates and carbonates include ammonium bicarbonate (NH4HCO3), ammonium carbonate ((NH4)2CO3), barium carbonate (BaCO3), cadmium carbonate (CdCO3), cesium carbonate (Cs2CO3), calcium bicarbonate (Ca(HCO3)3), calcium carbonate (CaCO3), cerium carbonate (Ce2(CO3)3), cobalt carbonate (CoCO3), copper carbonate (CuCO3), iron carbonate (FeCO3), lead carbonate (PbCO3), lanthanum carbonate (La2(CO3)3), lithium carbonate (Li2CO3), magnesium carbonate (MgCO3), manganese carbonate (MnCO3), nickel carbonate (NiCO3), potassium bicarbonate (KHCO3), potassium carbonate (K2CO3), silver carbonate (Ag2CO3), sodium bicarbonate (NaHCO3), sodium carbonate (Na2CO3), strontium carbonate (SrCO3), and zinc carbonate (ZnCO3). Metal carbonyls are coordination complexes formed between transition metals and carbon monoxide (CO) ligands. These complexes are covalent in nature. Examples of metal carbonyls include chromium hexacarbonyl (Cr(CO)6), cobalt octacarbonyl (Co2(CO)8), iron pentacarbonyl (Fe(CO)5), manganese decacarbonyl (Mn2(CO)10), molybdenum hexacarbonyl (Mo(CO)6), nickel tetracarbonyl (Ni(CO)4), and tungsten hexacarbonyl (W(CO)6). Other inorganic carbon compounds include salts and complexes of carbon-containing polyatomic ions such as cyanide, isocyanide, cyanate, and thiocyanate. Examples include ammonium thiocyanate (NH4SCN), calcium cyanamide (CaNCN), cobalt thiocyanate (Co(SCN)2), copper cyanide (CuCN), cyanic acid polymers ((HCNO)x), cyanamide (NH2CN), cyanic acid (HCNO), cyanogen ((CN)2), bromine cyanide (BrCN), chlorine cyanide (ClCN), hydrogen cyanide (HCN), potassium cyanate (KOCN), potassium cyanide (KCN), potassium ferricyanide (K3Fe(CN)6), potassium ferrocyanide (K4Fe(CN)6), potassium thiocyanate (KSCN), Prussian blue (Fe4(Fe(CN)6)3), silver cyanide (AgCN), sodium cyanate (NaOCN), sodium cyanide (NaCN), sodium nitroprusside (Na3Fe(CN)5NO), sodium thiocyanate (NaSCN), and thiocyanogen ((SCN)2). Carbides are binary compounds of carbon with elements that are less electronegative than carbon. Examples include boron carbide (B4C), calcium carbide (CaC2), silicon carbide (SiC), tantalum carbide (TaC), titanium carbide (TiC), and tungsten carbide (WC). The study of carbon allotropes, such as diamond, graphite, and fullerenes, has expanded significantly since the discovery of buckminsterfullerene (C60) in 1985. Fullerenes and their derivatives include inclusion compounds, where an ion is encapsulated within the carbon shell of a fullerene. For instance, a lithium ion trapped within buckminsterfullerene is denoted as Li+@C60. These complexes can pair with counterions to form salts. Alloys Several alloys contain carbon, with carbon steel being the most well-known. Other iron-carbon alloys include anthracite iron, cast iron, pig iron, wrought iron, and spiegeleisen (which also contains manganese). Stellite is an alloy of carbon with cobalt, chromium, and tungsten. These alloys can, to some extent, be considered carbides. Formation of Carbon Compounds In organic chemistry, carbon, oxygen, and hydrogen are the three most important elements. Each of these elements forms bonds of different valencies: carbon forms tetravalent bonds, oxygen forms divalent bonds, and hydrogen forms monovalent bonds.
